items.stem: Define the term 'Ansoff's matrix'.
items.answer: A model showing four growth strategies — market penetration, market development, product development and diversification — according to whether products and markets are existing or new, with risk increasing away from existing products and markets.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, a model showing four growth strategies — market penetration, market development, product development and diversification — according to whether products and markets are existing or new, with risk increasing away from existing products and markets. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain why market penetration is usually the least risky growth strategy.
items.answer: The business already knows its product and customers, so it builds on existing knowledge, brands and distribution.
items.markingKey: 1 mark existing knowledge; 1 mark lower uncertainty. [2]

items.stem: Explain one reason why a business might choose diversification despite its risk.
items.answer: To spread risk across markets if its existing market is declining, or to exploit high-growth opportunities and use spare resources.
items.markingKey: 1 mark reason; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: A global brand has threatened to cancel its contract after a report on long working hours. Nusantara Apparel Tbk, a public limited company in Indonesia with about 4,000 employees, makes sportswear under contract for global brands. Explain how Nusantara Apparel could increase market penetration of its sportswear in Indonesia.
items.answer: Points to develop for Nusantara Apparel: market penetration = existing products, existing markets; promotion and loyalty schemes; competitive pricing; wider distribution.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: market penetration = existing products, existing markets. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Nusantara Apparel: clothing manufacturing, about 4,000 employees, public limited company in Indonesia; a global brand has threatened to cancel its contract after a report on long working hours). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Nusantara Apparel, e.g. promotion and loyalty schemes; competitive pricing; wider distribution. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Nusantara Apparel Tbk is a public limited company based in Jakarta, Indonesia. It makes sportswear under contract for global brands and employs about 4,000 people. A global brand has threatened to cancel its contract after a report on long working hours. Discuss whether Nusantara Apparel should diversify by launching its own brand of affordable sportswear in the Philippines.
items.answer: For: spreads risk; growth potential; uses core competencies. Against: highest-risk strategy; lack of experience; large investment. Judgement: the decision for Nusantara Apparel depends mainly on market research evidence, and also on available finance.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [2]: uses case evidence (Nusantara Apparel: clothing manufacturing, about 4,000 employees, public limited company in Indonesia; a global brand has threatened to cancel its contract after a report on long working hours). AO3 Analysis [4]: arguments for, e.g. spreads risk; growth potential; uses core competencies; arguments against, e.g. highest-risk strategy; lack of experience; large investment. AO4 Evaluation [4]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on market research evidence; available finance; links with existing competencies. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Nusantara Apparel, not a generic one. [12]

items.stem: According to Ansoff's matrix, which growth strategy usually carries the highest risk?
items.answer: Diversification
items.markingKey: Diversification. New products in new markets: least knowledge and experience.

items.stem: Which of the following best defines 'product development'?
options: Factors that push an organisation towards a proposed change, e.g. new technology, competitive pressure or cost savings.

A model showing four growth strategies — market penetration, market development, product development and diversification — according to whether products and markets are existing or new, with risk increasing away from existing products and markets.
Selling new or modified products in existing markets.
Increasing sales of existing products in existing markets, e.g. through promotion or price cuts.
items.answer: Selling new or modified products in existing markets.
items.markingKey: product development: Selling new or modified products in existing markets.

items.answer: Uses existing product knowledge.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant advantage, e.g. uses existing product knowledge; larger market and growth; spreads risk across countries. 1 mark: explained in the context of BatikPay (financial technology). [2]

items.stem: Explain how Ansoff's matrix can be used with other strategic tools.
items.answer: SWOT and PESTLE identify opportunities and risks for each option; investment appraisal and decision trees then evaluate the chosen options.
items.markingKey: 1 mark link to analysis tools; 1 mark link to choice tools. [2]

items.stem: A global brand has threatened to cancel its contract after a report on long working hours. items.answer: option 1 market development; option 2 diversification
items.markingKey: option 1: market development; option 2: diversification [2]; ranking by distance from existing products/markets: option 2 > option 1 [1]. [3]

items.stem: Based in Bangkok, Siam Ready Meals Co. Ltd (private limited company) produces chilled and frozen ready meals for supermarkets and convenience stores. items.answer: option 1 diversification; option 2 product development; option 3 market development
items.markingKey: option 1: diversification; option 2: product development; option 3: market development [3]; ranking by distance from existing products/markets: option 1 > option 2 > option 3 [1]. [4]

items.stem: Define the term 'force field analysis'.
items.answer: A decision-making technique (Lewin) that identifies and scores the driving forces for a change and the restraining forces against it, to judge whether the change is likely to succeed.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, a decision-making technique (Lewin) that identifies and scores the driving forces for a change and the restraining forces against it, to judge whether the change is likely to succeed. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain how managers can use force field analysis to help implement change.
items.answer: They can strengthen driving forces (e.g. communicate benefits) and reduce restraining forces (e.g. training, consultation), shifting the balance towards change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark strengthen drivers; 1 mark weaken restrainers. [2]

items.stem: Explain one limitation of force field analysis.
items.answer: The scores given to forces are subjective and may be biased, so the result may not reflect reality.
items.markingKey: 1 mark subjectivity; 1 mark consequence. [2]

items.stem: A major US retailer has asked it to cut delivery times from twelve weeks to six. Mekong Furniture JSC, a joint stock company in Vietnam with about 1,200 employees, makes wooden and rattan furniture for large retailers in the USA and Europe. Explain how force field analysis could help Mekong Furniture introduce a new IT system.
items.answer: Points to develop for Mekong Furniture: force field compares driving and restraining forces; identifies resistance from staff; plans training and communication to reduce restraining forces; judges likelihood of success.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: force field compares driving and restraining forces. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Mekong Furniture: furniture manufacturing, about 1,200 employees, joint stock company in Vietnam; a major US retailer has asked it to cut delivery times from twelve weeks to six). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Mekong Furniture, e.g. identifies resistance from staff; plans training and communication to reduce restraining forces; judges likelihood of success. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.answer: For: change is favoured; drivers may grow; restrainers can be reduced. Against: narrow margin; subjective scores; risk of failure. Judgement: the decision for Deccan Auto depends mainly on ability to reduce restraining forces, and also on the cost of failure.

items.stem: Desert Bloom Hotels plc is a public limited company based in Dubai, the United Arab Emirates. It operates fourteen four- and five-star hotels and employs about 3,100 people. items.answer: Scores are subjective.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: relevant disadvantage, e.g. scores are subjective; may oversimplify; time-consuming. 1 mark: explained in the context of Desert Bloom (hospitality). [2]

items.stem: Explain why reducing restraining forces may be more effective than increasing driving forces.
items.answer: Pushing harder can increase resistance and tension; removing obstacles such as fear or lack of skills makes change smoother.
items.markingKey: 1 mark extra pressure creates resistance; 1 mark removing obstacles. [2]

items.stem: Tejo Mobility SA is considering introducing a new ERP system. Managers score each force from 1 (weak) to 5 (strong): driving forces — customer demand 4, government grants 3, new technology available 4; restraining forces — trade union opposition 3, lack of skills 5, risk of disruption 2. Calculate the total of each set of forces and state what the analysis suggests.
items.answer: Driving 11, restraining 10: change favoured
items.markingKey: Driving = 4 + 3 + 4 = 11 [1]; restraining = 3 + 5 + 2 = 10 [1]; drivers exceed restrainers, so change likely to succeed [1]. [3]

items.stem: Define the term 'decision tree'.
items.answer: A diagram that sets out the options available to a decision-maker, the possible outcomes of each, their probabilities and financial results, so that expected values can be compared.
items.markingKey: 2 marks: full definition, a diagram that sets out the options available to a decision-maker, the possible outcomes of each, their probabilities and financial results, so that expected values can be compared. 1 mark: partial definition or relevant example only. [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage of using decision trees.
items.answer: They set out options and outcomes clearly and allow risk (probability) and return to be combined in a single expected value for comparison.
items.markingKey: 1 mark advantage; 1 mark explanation. [2]

items.stem: Explain why the option with the highest expected value may not be chosen.
items.answer: Expected value is an average; managers may be risk-averse and avoid an option with a chance of a large loss, or qualitative factors may matter.
items.markingKey: 1 mark average/risk; 1 mark risk attitude or qualitative. [2]

items.stem: Based in Singapore, Lumen Robotics plc (public limited company) designs and builds robots used on factory assembly lines. The business has around 2,400 employees. items.answer: Points to develop for Lumen Robotics: EV is a weighted average; probabilities and payoffs are estimates; ignores attitude to risk; ignores qualitative factors and timing of cash flows.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: EV is a weighted average. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Lumen Robotics: industrial engineering, about 2,400 employees, public limited company in Singapore; shareholders are pressing for higher dividends while engineers want more spending on research). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Lumen Robotics, e.g. probabilities and payoffs are estimates; ignores attitude to risk; ignores qualitative factors and timing of cash flows. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Tejo Mobility SA is a public limited company based in Lisbon, Portugal. It assembles electric scooters and e-bikes for sale across the European Union and employs about 600 people. Battery supply problems from Asia have delayed several large orders. Explain the risks to Tejo Mobility of launching electric cargo bikes for delivery firms in Brazil, using Ansoff's matrix.
items.answer: Points to develop for Tejo Mobility: new product in new market is diversification; lack of market knowledge; lack of product experience; large investment with uncertain demand.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: new product in new market is diversification. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Tejo Mobility: vehicle manufacturing, about 600 employees, public limited company in Portugal; battery supply problems from Asia have delayed several large orders). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Tejo Mobility, e.g. lack of market knowledge; lack of product experience; large investment with uncertain demand. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [4]

items.stem: Based in Colombo, Lanka Tea Estates plc (public limited company) grows, processes and packs tea on its own estates. The business has around 5,000 employees. Many young workers are leaving the estates for jobs in the cities. (a) Define 'market development'. (b) Explain one advantage to Lanka Tea of a strategy of market development by selling packaged tea in Russia.
items.answer: (a) Selling existing products in new markets, e.g. new countries or new customer segments. (b) Uses existing product knowledge.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark partial, 2 marks full definition [2] (b) 1 mark point (uses existing product knowledge; larger market and growth; spreads risk across countries), 1 mark explanation, 1 mark application to Lanka Tea [3]

items.stem: Based in Colombo, Lanka Tea Estates plc (public limited company) grows, processes and packs tea on its own estates. The business has around 5,000 employees. Many young workers are leaving the estates for jobs in the cities. Using the case and your own knowledge, using Ansoff's matrix, evaluate the most suitable growth strategy for Lanka Tea.
items.answer: For: market penetration is low risk; market development uses existing products in Russia; product development builds on customers with ready-to-drink iced tea. Against: penetration limited in saturated markets; development needs market knowledge; diversification is highest risk. Judgement: the decision for Lanka Tea depends mainly on its resources and core competencies, and also on the growth of its current market.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [3]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [3]: uses case evidence (Lanka Tea: agriculture and food, about 5,000 employees, public limited company in Sri Lanka; many young workers are leaving the estates for jobs in the cities). AO3 Analysis [6]: arguments for, e.g. market penetration is low risk; market development uses existing products in Russia; product development builds on customers with ready-to-drink iced tea; arguments against, e.g. penetration limited in saturated markets; development needs market knowledge; diversification is highest risk. AO4 Evaluation [8]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on its resources and core competencies; the growth of its current market; its attitude to risk. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Lanka Tea, not a generic one. [20]

items.stem: In force field analysis, which is most likely to be a restraining force against introducing new technology?
options: Fear of job losses among employees
items.answer: Fear of job losses among employees
items.markingKey: Fear of job losses among employees. Restraining forces resist change.

items.answer: Opportunity: identifies sources of resistance. Threat: scores are subjective.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark point, 1 mark application to Mekong Furniture: furniture manufacturing, 1,200 employees). items.stem: Lumen Robotics plc is a public limited company based in Singapore. It designs and builds robots used on factory assembly lines and employs about 2,400 people. Shareholders are pressing for higher dividends while engineers want more spending on research. Explain how force field analysis could help Lumen Robotics introduce a new IT system.
items.answer: Points to develop for Lumen Robotics: force field compares driving and restraining forces; identifies resistance from staff; plans training and communication to reduce restraining forces; judges likelihood of success.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: force field compares driving and restraining forces. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Lumen Robotics: industrial engineering, about 2,400 employees, public limited company in Singapore; shareholders are pressing for higher dividends while engineers want more spending on research). items.stem: Based in Toronto, Maple Learning Inc. (private limited company) runs an online tutoring and test-preparation platform for school students. The business has around 260 employees. Venture capital investors expect it to become profitable within two years. Evaluate the usefulness of force field analysis to Maple Learning when making a major strategic change.
items.answer: For: structured view of pressures; identifies resistance; supports planning of change. Against: subjective scores; does not show financial return; forces may change. Judgement: the decision for Maple Learning depends mainly on who scores the forces, and also on use alongside investment appraisal.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. AO2 Application [2]: uses case evidence (Maple Learning: education technology, about 260 employees, private limited company in Canada; venture capital investors expect it to become profitable within two years). AO4 Evaluation [4]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on who scores the forces; use alongside investment appraisal; the complexity of the change. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Maple Learning, not a generic one. [12]

items.stem: Which business term is described here: "A point on a decision tree, shown as a circle, where different outcomes may occur, each with a probability."
items.answer: chance node

items.answer: Probabilities are estimates.

items.answer: option 1: EV $250k; option 2: EV $362.5k

items.stem: Savanna Fresh Ltd must choose between two options (or do nothing). items.answer: Spreads risk across markets.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain one reason why a business might choose diversification despite its risk. (b) Explain how Ansoff's matrix can be used with other strategic tools.
items.answer: (a) To spread risk across markets if its existing market is declining, or to exploit high-growth opportunities and use spare resources. (b) SWOT and PESTLE identify opportunities and risks for each option; investment appraisal and decision trees then evaluate the chosen options.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark reason; 1 mark explanation. [2] (b) 1 mark link to analysis tools; 1 mark link to choice tools. [2]

items.stem: The owners want to double the number of cafés within three years. Café Cordillera SAS, a private limited company in Colombia with about 900 employees, roasts coffee and runs a chain of 60 cafés. items.answer: Points to develop for Café Cordillera: market penetration = existing products, existing markets; promotion and loyalty schemes; competitive pricing; wider distribution.
items.markingKey: AO1 Knowledge [1]: market penetration = existing products, existing markets. AO2 Application [1]: answer uses the case (Café Cordillera: food and drink retail, about 900 employees, private limited company in Colombia; the owners want to double the number of cafés within three years). items.stem: Based in Cairo, Nile Pharma plc (public limited company) manufactures generic medicines for hospitals and pharmacies in Africa and the Middle East. The directors of Nile Pharma are considering: option 1, selling more generic medicines in Egypt; option 2, selling generic medicines in East Africa. items.answer: option 1 market penetration; option 2 market development
items.markingKey: option 1: market penetration; option 2: market development [2]; ranking by distance from existing products/markets: option 2 > option 1 [1]. [3]

items.answer: option 1 product development; option 2 market penetration; option 3 diversification
items.markingKey: option 1: product development; option 2: market penetration; option 3: diversification [3]; ranking by distance from existing products/markets: option 3 > option 1 > option 2 [1]. [4]

items.stem: Based in Cape Town, Cape Brew Co. (Pty) Ltd (private limited company) brews craft beers and low-sugar soft drinks sold through bars and supermarkets. items.answer: (a) Selling new or modified products in existing markets. (b) Uses existing product knowledge.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark partial, 2 marks full definition [2] (b) 1 mark point (uses existing product knowledge; larger market and growth; spreads risk across countries), 1 mark explanation, 1 mark application to Cape Brew [3]

items.stem: Andes Textil SA is a family-owned private company based in Lima, Peru. It makes premium alpaca knitwear for fashion retailers in North America and Japan and employs about 320 people. The founder is retiring and the new managing director wants to modernise production. (a) Define 'Ansoff's matrix'. (b) Explain one advantage to Andes Textil of a strategy of diversification by launching a range of alpaca home furnishings in China. (c) Analyse how Andes Textil could increase market penetration of its alpaca knitwear in Peru. (d) Using Ansoff's matrix, evaluate the most suitable growth strategy for Andes Textil.
items.answer: (a) A model showing four growth strategies — market penetration, market development, product development and diversification — according to whether products and markets are existing or new, with risk increasing away from existing products and markets. (b) Spreads risk across markets. (c) Market penetration = existing products, existing markets; promotion and loyalty schemes; competitive pricing; wider distribution. (d) For: market penetration is low risk; market development uses existing products in China; product development builds on customers with a range of alpaca home furnishings. Against: penetration limited in saturated markets; development needs market knowledge; diversification is highest risk. Judgement: the decision for Andes Textil depends mainly on its resources and core competencies, and also on the growth of its current market.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark partial, 2 marks full definition [2] (b) 1 mark point (spreads risk across markets; high growth potential; uses spare resources), 1 mark explanation, 1 mark application to Andes Textil [3] (c) AO1 Knowledge [2]: market penetration = existing products, existing markets. AO2 Application [2]: answer uses the case (Andes Textil: textile manufacturing, about 320 employees, family-owned private company in Peru; the founder is retiring and the new managing director wants to modernise production). AO3 Analysis [2]: developed chains of reasoning showing the consequence for Andes Textil, e.g. promotion and loyalty schemes; competitive pricing; wider distribution. Levels: L1 knowledge only; L2 applied to the case; L3 applied and analysed. [6] (d) AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. AO3 Analysis [3]: arguments for, e.g. market penetration is low risk; market development uses existing products in China; product development builds on customers with a range of alpaca home furnishings; arguments against, e.g. penetration limited in saturated markets; development needs market knowledge; diversification is highest risk. AO4 Evaluation [3]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on its resources and core competencies; the growth of its current market; its attitude to risk. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Andes Textil, not a generic one. [10]

items.stem: Which of the following best defines 'restraining forces'?
options: Selling existing products in new markets, e.g. new countries or new customer segments.
Factors that push an organisation towards a proposed change, e.g. new technology, competitive pressure or cost savings.
Factors that work against a proposed change, e.g. employee resistance, cost or lack of skills.
The current situation, maintained because the driving and restraining forces are balanced.
items.answer: Factors that work against a proposed change, e.g. employee resistance, cost or lack of skills.
items.markingKey: restraining forces: Factors that work against a proposed change, e.g. employee resistance, cost or lack of skills.

items.stem: Based in Jakarta, Nusantara Apparel Tbk (public limited company) makes sportswear under contract for global brands. The business has around 4,000 employees. items.stem: Based in Auckland, Kiwi Trails Ltd (private limited company) runs guided hiking, kayaking and cycling tours. The business has around 90 employees. Bookings are highly seasonal and most guides are employed only for the summer. (a) Define 'driving forces'. (b) Discuss whether Kiwi Trails should go ahead with a change when the driving forces only slightly exceed the restraining forces.
items.answer: (a) Factors that push an organisation towards a proposed change, e.g. new technology, competitive pressure or cost savings. (b) For: change is favoured; drivers may grow; restrainers can be reduced. Against: narrow margin; subjective scores; risk of failure. Judgement: the decision for Kiwi Trails depends mainly on ability to reduce restraining forces, and also on the cost of failure.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark partial, 2 marks full definition [2] (b) AO1 Knowledge [2]: relevant concepts/theory. AO3 Analysis [3]: arguments for, e.g. change is favoured; drivers may grow; restrainers can be reduced; arguments against, e.g. narrow margin; subjective scores; risk of failure. AO4 Evaluation [3]: a supported judgement that weighs the arguments, e.g. it depends on ability to reduce restraining forces; the cost of failure; strategic importance. Highest level needs a justified conclusion specific to Kiwi Trails, not a generic one. [10]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the probabilities used in a decision tree are often unreliable. (b) Explain one advantage of using decision trees.
items.answer: (a) They are usually estimated from past experience or market research, and the future may differ; managers may also be biased. (b) They set out options and outcomes clearly and allow risk (probability) and return to be combined in a single expected value for comparison.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark estimated; 1 mark reasons for error. [2] (b) 1 mark advantage; 1 mark explanation. [2]
